blocks.title: The whole yard, **caught up.**
body: Spring cleanup is the first visit of the year, and it gets the yard back to a clean start. We clear leaves, sticks and winter debris from the lawn and out of the beds, cut back last year's dead stems and ornamental grasses, recut the bed edges and blow off the drive and walks.

Then the lawn gets its first mow of the season. From there the yard is ready for [fresh mulch](/mulch-and-flower-beds/), [shrub trimming](/shrub-trimming/) or a spot on the [weekly mowing](/lawn-mowing/) route, whichever you want next.

blocks.title: From winter mess to **a first cut.**

steps.body: Leaves, sticks and debris come off the lawn and out of the beds, with a light hand around bulbs and perennials that are already coming up.

blocks.title: Good spring habits for **a Michigan yard.**
blocks.intro: A few things Michigan State University Extension says are worth knowing before anyone, us included, works a yard in early spring.

items.title: Rake light, not hard
items.body: Snow mold usually kills only the grass blades, not the plant, MSU says. A light pass with a leaf rake, not a garden rake, lifts the matted spots and helps the new growth come through.

items.title: Stay off soggy ground
items.body: Rolling or turning a heavy mower on saturated soil packs it down. MSU's advice is to wait until the soil dries rather than risk making the problem worse.

items.title: Leave some stems for the bees
items.body: Bees and other insects spend the winter in leaf litter and hollow perennial stems, and some stay put until June or July. MSU suggests working slowly, or setting cut stems aside where insects can still come out. Tell Rob if you want some left.

items.title: Check the salt line
items.body: MSU notes that de-icing salt can kill patches of grass over the winter. If the strip along the drive or walk has not greened up, it may need reseeding. Ask Rob about [new seed](/grading-and-new-lawns/) when he comes out.

blocks.title: Between soggy ground and **fast grass.**
body: Spring cleanup in Michigan sits between two things. Early on, a lot of yards are too wet to work without packing the soil or leaving ruts. Then the grass takes off: MSU Extension says the spring growth surge peaks in May or June. Getting the cleanup done in between means the first cut lands on a clean lawn.

Our shop is on Embury Road in Grand Blanc, and we do spring cleanups all over Grand Blanc and Grand Blanc Township. We also work around Genesee County and into north Oakland County, including [Fenton](/spring-cleanup-fenton-mi/), [Davison](/spring-cleanup-davison-mi/), [Burton](/spring-cleanup-burton-mi/) and [Clarkston](/spring-cleanup-clarkston-mi/).

faq.q: Do you do spring cleanups in Grand Blanc?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes does spring cleanups in Grand Blanc, Grand Blanc Township and across Genesee County. We clear winter debris from the lawn and beds, cut back old growth, recut the bed edges and give the lawn its first cut. Call or text Rob at [(810) 990-3040](tel:+18109903040) for a free estimate.

faq.q: When should I do a spring yard cleanup in Michigan?
faq.a: Once the ground has dried out enough to walk on without sinking in, and before the grass takes off. MSU Extension warns that rolling or driving on saturated soil compacts it, and says the spring growth surge usually peaks in May or June. In the beds, MSU suggests a slower touch early on, since some bees and butterflies are still sheltering in leaf litter and stems.

faq.q: What does a spring cleanup include?
faq.a: Leaves, sticks and winter debris cleared from the lawn and beds, last year's dead stems and ornamental grasses cut back, bed edges recut, the first mow of the season, and the drive and walks blown off. Rob goes over the list with you when he quotes it, and extras like mulch can be added.

faq.q: Should I rake my lawn in the spring?
faq.a: Lightly, and only where it needs it. MSU Extension recommends a leaf rake, not a garden rake, on matted or snow mold spots, to lift the dead blades so new growth can come through. Snow mold usually kills only the leaf tissue, so most of those spots recover as the soil warms.

faq.q: When should I cut back ornamental grasses and perennials?
faq.a: Late winter or early spring, before the new growth comes up. MSU Extension suggests leaving the stems standing through winter as shelter for bees and other helpful insects, then cutting them during the dormant season and setting them somewhere the insects can still come out. We cut them back as part of a spring cleanup.

faq.q: Can you mulch the beds during a spring cleanup?
faq.a: Yes, and spring is a natural time for it, with the beds cleared and edged. We lay fresh mulch in black, brown or red, with fabric underneath where you want it. See [mulch and flower bed makeovers](/mulch-and-flower-beds/) for how that part goes.

faq.q: How much does a spring cleanup cost?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the yard, how many beds there are and how much winter left behind. Rob comes out, looks at it and quotes you a price before any work starts. The estimate is free.
